title: Use #[expect] instead of #[allow] for lint suppressions
description:
## What

#[expect(...)] stabilized in Rust 1.81; the MSRV is now 1.88. It behaves like #[allow] but warns when the lint it suppresses does NOT fire, so a suppression that has become unnecessary is reported instead of lingering.

The workspace has nine such suppressions:

- 7x #[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]
- 1x #[allow(clippy::struct_excessive_bools)]
- 1x #[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]

## Why it is worth the churn

The too_many_arguments suppressions are the interesting ones. Several sit on verify entry points whose argument lists are exactly the thing the workspace keeps reconsidering -- verify_tls_server_dane added a ninth argument, and DaneConfig was introduced partly to avoid a tenth. If one of those functions is later refactored to take a config struct, the suppression becomes stale and nothing says so. #[expect] says so.

This is small. It is filed because it is the kind of hygiene that is free at the moment someone is already touching lint attributes and annoying to retrofit later.

## Caution

Do not convert a suppression whose lint fires only under some feature combination -- #[expect] would then warn in the combinations where the lint is quiet. Check each site against --all-features and the default feature set before converting, or leave it as #[allow] with a comment saying why.

## Acceptance

[ ] Each of the nine sites either converted to #[expect] or left as #[allow] with a recorded reason
[ ] clippy clean under the default feature set AND --all-features after conversion
